text: Rosa Vidal to Ivana Horvat: “Welcome, Mayor. I hear the mill's stirring up talk. People come here to eat and drink, they tell me things. I know what worries this town.”
Petar Ilić to Rosa Vidal: “I'm Petar Ilić, baker from here. I heard you might help with the mill. We need island flour again, not this mainland stuff. What do you know about getting it running?”
Ivana Horvat to Rosa Vidal: “Good to see you, Rosa. The mill project has raised some questions. What are people saying about it?”

Rosa Vidal to Ivana Horvat: “The mill's been on everyone's mind. Petar's right - we need island flour. I've heard people are interested. This is exactly the kind of thing we should be talking through here at the inn.”
The 18:00 ferry docked.
Ivana Horvat to Rosa Vidal: “The mill is an important question. Before we make any decisions, I think we should have a proper survey done. We need good information.”
Rosa Vidal to Ivana Horvat: “You're right about needing good information on the mill. Come, sit down - let's talk about what we actually know. Can I get you something to eat?”
Rosa Vidal bought bread for 1.
Petar Ilić bought bread for 1.

Rosa Vidal ate bread.

Ivana Horvat to Rosa Vidal: “Hello Rosa. I'm here to listen and understand what the town needs. What's been on people's minds lately?”
Ivana Horvat ate bread.

Rosa Vidal to Ivana Horvat: “Welcome. You're asking the right question. People want the inn to matter again - to be where decisions happen, where news breaks. That's what I'm working toward.”
The 19:00 ferry docked.
Luka Babić went to the harbor inn.
Ivana Horvat to Rosa Vidal: “Thank you for the welcome. I'm interested in understanding how the community works here. What matters most to people right now?”

Rosa Vidal to Ivana Horvat: “Welcome to Ferry Town. What matters is keeping things running and knowing who can be counted on. The inn's always been where people come to figure things out. You'll learn fast enough.”
Ivana Horvat to Rosa Vidal: “Thank you for the welcome. I'm interested in understanding how things work here, especially what matters to the community. I'd like to learn more about the town.”
Rosa Vidal to Ivana Horvat: “Welcome to Ferry Town. I'm Rosa, I run this place. You'll find most of what matters happens right here at the inn. What brings you to the island?”

Petar Ilić and Vesna Marić talked at the harbor inn. Petar Ilić: “You're Vesna, yeah? Heard you rent rooms. I need something longer than three nights at the inn, but I need to know the rates first.” Vesna Marić: “Fifty coins a week. Quiet place, no trouble. You look like someone who works early.” Petar Ilić: “I'm a baker. The rates are fair. But the room—does it stay at fifty, or does that change?” Vesna Marić: “Why would it change? You pay on time, it stays the same.” Petar Ilić: “Good. I'll let you know by tomorrow.”

Rosa Vidal to Ivana Horvat: “Welcome to the inn. I'm Rosa. You picked a good time to visit - we've got some interesting people here tonight. What brings you to the island?”
The 20:00 ferry docked.
Ivana Horvat to Rosa Vidal: “Thank you, Rosa. I'm here on some municipal business. It's nice to be out of the rain for a moment. How are things on the island these days?”
Rosa Vidal to Ivana Horvat: “Things are steady, Ivana. It's good to have you back in here out of that rain. What kind of municipal business brings you by tonight?”
Ivana Horvat to Rosa Vidal: “Hello Rosa. Just needed to get out of the rain for a bit. How are people feeling about things these days?”
Rosa Vidal to Ivana Horvat: “Good to see you, Ivana. People are managing, same as always. What's on your mind these days?”

Ana Perić and Luka Babić talked at the harbor inn. Ana Perić: “You're Luka, right. I heard about the mill roof. How long has it been sitting like that.” Luka Babić: “Since January. The council talks about it. The roof doesn't care about talking.” Ana Perić: “That's frustrating. Have you asked them directly what's holding it up.” Luka Babić: “I know what's holding it up. Nothing moves until someone decides to move. I'm not good at deciding for other people.” Ana Perić: “Sounds like there's a real gap between what people say they'll do and what actually happens here. That kind of thing interests me.” Luka Babić: “Then you'll see plenty.”

action.text: Rosa, good to see you too. It's been a long day indeed. The town seems quiet tonight despite the rain. How are things here at the inn?

text: Ivana Horvat went to sleep at the harbor inn.

Rosa Vidal reflected: Back on the island with a suitcase and forty coins, three nights paid at the harbor inn. Feels strange to be a guest in the room I used to know the smell of. But the day gave me something: three new faces all landed at once, and by evening all three were sitting in the same room. Ana Perić asks the kind of questions that need real answers - she told me about Henrik, the mill shut two months back, him gone, money missing. That's a thread I want to hold. Ivana Horvat is watching how the town runs, who decides what, and writing it down behind her eyes. Petar Ilić from the bakery is hunting flour suppliers, which means he'll be back to the inn every day until he finds one, and that's a regular. The mill closing and a baker without flour - those two facts belong together and nobody said it out loud today. I said nothing. I'm keeping the ledger current in my head. Thirty-eight coins and no work is a short rope, so tomorrow I need either a wage or a reason for the innkeeper to want me here. The inn was the middle of this town once. Three strangers under one roof is how it starts again.
Petar Ilić now thinks of Rosa Vidal: “Runs the inn, met me kindly, offered without me begging. Says she can help with the mill and suppliers. I was gruff with her and she didn't flinch. That counts.”

Petar Ilić reflected: Came off the ferry with a suitcase and forty coins, which is a strange thing for a man who was born here. Three nights at Rosa's inn, two left now. Rosa Vidal met me warm, warmer than I deserved before I'd said anything civil, and she says she can help me get at the mill question. I told her plain what I want: island flour again, not the mainland sacks I've been hauling. I did not tell her I've been paying more for those sacks than the bread brings back. A year of that. My father's oven is still lit and I intend to keep it that way, but the ledger says otherwise and the ledger doesn't argue. Met Ivana Horvat, newcomer, full of questions about how things run here — polite, watching everything. Vesna Marić I know a little. Ana Perić has the Gazette, which means she knows who owes who. Two people worth knowing, both women who trade in information, and I've never been good at trading anything but bread. No job, no staff, nobody who'll stay past a fortnight, and I still say that's on them. Mostly.

Ivana Horvat reflected: Rain the whole day. I came off the ferry with a suitcase, forty coins, three nights at Rosa's inn — now thirty-eight and two nights. I spent the day listening rather than talking, which is what I should have done my first term. Rosa Vidal runs the inn and lets you know she hears everything; that is half boast, half warning. Petar Ilić from the bakery is hunting suppliers and Vesna Marić was already offering him a room before his boots were dry — people move fast here when there is coin in it. Ana Perić has the Gazette, which means she decides what the mill is about before anyone votes on it. Nobody asked me for a position today and I gave none. The survey is still out and the survey is still doing its work, which is buying time. If I keep my mouth closed until the numbers come back, the vote falls after the election and no one can hang the mill around my neck either way. I need income soon; two nights of roof is not a plan.

Luka Babić reflected: Off the ferry, suitcase, forty coins, three nights bought at Rosa's inn. Took the mill hand work, three coins a shift. Spent the day looking at the roof more than talking. It's rotten in two places and the ridge beam is sound. A week of proper work with two pairs of hands and it holds through winter. I said none of that. Ana from the Gazette came at me with questions before she'd lifted anything, wanting the roof as a story. Petar at the bakery wants flour and is asking round for suppliers, which is honest enough of him. A woman called Ivana talks about governance. I've heard that kind of talk before at home. The roof never got fixed by talk. I'll wait and see who picks up a tool. If they form a council over it I'll let them, and the flour will still be mine to grind or not.

Ana Perić reflected: First day. Off the ferry with a suitcase and forty coins, three nights at Rosa's inn. Spent two coins on nothing much and I'm down to thirty-eight with two nights left, which is a clock I don't like hearing tick. But the day gave me something: Henrik gone two months, money missing with him, and the mill shut. Rosa knows everyone and seems happy to point me at people. Luka told me exactly what's wrong with this place and then told me he won't say it to the council. That gap is the story - a man who can name the rot and won't open his mouth. Ivana Horvat came off the same ferry asking about governance, which either makes her a source or a competitor, and I'd like to know which before she knows what I am. Petar at the bakery I've barely met. There's dock work if I need coins, and I will need coins. Nothing here matters yet, and that's the thing that frightens me - that I crossed water for a closed mill and a leaking roof. But missing money is missing money. Somebody on this island knows where Henrik went.
Vesna Marić now thinks of Petar Ilić: “Baker, direct, wants something more than three nights. No smell of trouble on him yet. Bakers keep hours, and people who keep hours pay on time.”

Vesna Marić reflected: Back with a suitcase and forty coins, sleeping in Rosa's inn like a stranger in my own town. Thirty-eight now. Two nights left paid. The room above the chandlery is sitting empty and that's the thing that keeps me awake, not the coins. Three came off the ferry today - Ivana, Petar, Ana. The baker, Petar, was the only one who asked me anything straight: what do I charge, is it longer than three nights. I didn't give him a number. Let him ask twice. He didn't look like the sort who slides out a window with the rent owing, but I've been wrong about better-dressed men. Didn't speak to the two women. Rosa took my coins without a word, which is the most I can ask of anybody.
Day 1 ended.
The weather turned to clear.
